'''''Nassella''''', or '''needlegrass''', is a [[New World]] genus of over 100 perennial [[bunchgrass]]es found from [[North America]] through [[South America]]. The Latin word ''nassa'' refers to "a basket with a narrow neck".<ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?8738,9138 ''Nassella''.] ''The Jepson Manual''.</ref> It is usually considered segregate from the genus ''[[Stipa]]'' and includes many New World species formerly classified in that genus.<ref>Barkworth, M. E. [http://herbarium.usu.edu/stipeae/nassella.htm ''Nassella'' E.Desv.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061205012508/http://herbarium.usu.edu/stipeae/nassella.htm |date=2006-12-05 }} ''Stipeae Pages''. Intermountain Herbarium, [[Utah State University]]. June 13, 2003.</ref> As of 2011, ''[[The Jepson Manual]]'' includes ''Nassella'' within ''Stipa''.<ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=45644 ''Stipa pulchra''.] ''The Jepson Manual''.</ref>

''Nasella'' is characterized by strongly overlapping lemma margins and reduced, veinless paleae.  The lemma tips are fused into the "crown", a short membrane that surrounds the base of the lemma.  The rim of the crown usually has hairs.

Many species form both cross-pollinating and self-pollinating florets in the terminal panicle.  The self-pollinating florets have 1–3 small anthers; the cross-pollinating florets have 3 longer anthers.  Some species have self-pollinating inflorescences hidden in their basal leaf sheaths.  These hidden inflorescences lack glumes and usually lack awns.

Some species, especially ''[[Nassella neesiana]]'' and ''[[Nassella tenuissima]]'', are considered invasive pests, as the grass is not properly digested by ruminants.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=458 | title=GISD }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/species.php?sc=463 | title=GISD }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225109211 |via=[[ResearchGate]]|doi=10.1007/s10530-010-9905-6 |title=The potential global distribution of the invasive weed Nassella neesiana under current and future climates |year=2012 |last1=Bourdôt |first1=Graeme W. |last2=Lamoureaux |first2=Shona L. |last3=Watt |first3=Michael S. |last4=Manning |first4=Lucy K. |last5=Kriticos |first5=Darren J. |journal=Biological Invasions |volume=14 |issue=8 |pages=1545–1556 |bibcode=2012BiInv..14.1545B |s2cid=14852104 }}</ref>

==Diversity==
As of 2001, there were about 116 species in this genus.<ref name=bark>Barkworth, M. E. and M. A. Torres. (2001). [https://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/1223891?uid=3739560&uid=2129&uid=2&uid=70&uid=4&uid=3739256&sid=21102347554001 Distribution and diagnostic characters of ''Nassella'' (Poaceae: Stipeae).] ''Taxon'' 50(2) Golden Jubilee Part 4, 439–68.</ref>

===California species===
*''[[Nassella pulchra]]'' – purple needlegrass; currently reclassified as ''Stipa pulchra''.
::*A [[California native plants#Common Grasses of California|native grass of California]] that was once a dominant species in California [[grassland]]s before [[invasive plant|invasive]] European grasses became dominant. The seeds were an important food source for many of the [[Indigenous peoples of California]]. Today, the bunchgrass is the State Grass of California and plays an important role in native grassland restoration and erosion control.<ref>[http://www.library.ca.gov/history/cahinsig.cfm "History and Culture: State Insignia"], ''[[California State Library]]'', December 8, 2006.</ref>

*''[[Nassella lepida]]'' – foothill needlegrass; currently reclassified as ''Stipa lepida''.
::*A native [[bunchgrass]] of California and [[Baja California]].

*''[[Nassella cernua]]'' – nodding needlegrass; currently reclassified as ''Stipa cernua''.
::*A native bunchgrass of California, Northwestern Mexico, and the [[Western United States]].

===Horticultural species===
*''[[Nassella tenuissima]]'' – Mexican feathergrass.
::*An attractive, drought-tolerant bunchgrass with fine leaves and a narrow inflorescence that sways gracefully in the wind. However, it readily escapes from cultivation and takes hold in disturbed areas, natural areas, and in sidewalk cracks, driveways, and tree wells. It is an [[invasive species]] in [[California]] and [[Oregon]].
